newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia completes Alpha space module tests on time.
newsitem.headline: Russia completes Alpha space module tests on time.

text.p: Russia's Khrunichev space centre said on Monday it had finished ground tests on the first module of the new Alpha international space station and planned to ship it, on schedule, to the Baikonur cosmodrome in December.

Russia's ability to meet its promises on the $100-billion project has been in doubt since February, when Moscow postponed the launch of the first module, the functional cargo block, to June 1998 from November this year.

The delay, caused mainly by Russia's financial problems, provoked protests from the United States and other Western participants who warned that the entire Alpha project, to be built in stages by 2003, would be held up.

Some Western officials said Russia should be dumped from the team even though Alpha has been conceived as a replacement to the 11-year-old Russian Mir station, the world's only orbiting research centre.
Khrunichev senior programme manager Sergei Shayevich said, however, that the Russians were meeting the new schedule.
"We have installed U.S. equipment on the FGB (cargo block) and adapted it to Russia-made systems," he told a news conference.

He added that the cargo block would be upgraded to allow it to dock with cargo and manned craft until the next Russian-made accommodation module, the third component of Alpha and specially designed for docking, goes into orbit in December 1998.
"Over the next seven months we will undertake ground tests of the equipment together with our U.S. partners. These tests will make Alpha even more reliable," Shayevich said.
The 23.5-tonne cargo block module cost $190 million and is planned as one of the three anchor components of Alpha.

Last month, the Russian Space Agency said Russia's 12 of Alpha's 36 modules would cost $3.2 billion. The United States plans to built 18 modules worth $17.2 billion. The European Space Agency, Japan, Canada and Italy are also contributing.

Shayevich said Khrunichev was at present paying for the construction of the accommodation module, where the cosmonauts will live and work. In April, the Russian government promised 1.5 trillion roubles ($261 million) to fund the construction.
"We hope to get this money very soon," Shayevich said.
He also said that a technical facility for the cargo block was ready waiting for it at Baikonur.
"(The module) will have pre-launch tests at Baikonur, including its anti-meteorite defence system which will be more efficient than that of Mir," he said.
Shayevich said that a heavy booster Proton, which will take the module to a 220-km (137-mile) orbit, was being assembled on schedule. The booster will be delivered to Baikonur in August.
